..
KEY MESSAGE 1...We enter into an unsettled pattern once again 
today with daily chances for showers and thunderstorms into at 
least mid week. Upper level trough currently in the Midwest will
dive SE'wards into the Tennessee River Valley today eventually 
stalling as an upper level ridge blocks this troughs forward 
progress. At the mid levels, will see multiple shortwaves round 
the base of this trough promoting periods of lift across ENC and
the offshore waters with the first weak mid level shortwave 
tracking along the coast starting this morning with additional 
shortwaves coming in from the west this afternoon and again on 
Mon/Tue. At the surface, closed low in the Midwest will 
gradually shift E'wards into the Ohio River Valley today with 
its associated surface front stalling just to the west. These 
features, in addition to the sea breeze each afternoon/evening, 
will be the main forcing present for a notable increase in 
precip chances. 

There are two areas of focus for shower and thunderstorm 
activity today. The first is isolated to scattered showers 
along and behind a N'ward moving warm front/coastal trough with 
much of the activity occuring offshore and areas east of Hwy 
17. We should still be too dry aloft inland as the boundary 
moves through, so thunder chances remain low inland Sun morning.
Proximity to the gulf stream could allow isolated to scattered 
showers and thunderstorms to reach coastal communities south of 
Oregon Inlet. The second will be in the afternoon/evening with 
shower and thunderstorm activity coming in from the west 
associated with the stalling upper trough. Cloud cover will play
a big role in how high instability can truly get, but with the 
dewpoints rising there should be enough instability entering the
region for 1000-2000 J/kg of MLCAPE Sunday. While shear is not 
too impressive with the unidirectional SE flow, the combination 
of long, skinny CAPEs, PWATs over 2", and slow storm motions 
could result in heavy rainfall rates and wet microbursts where 
storms develop. The best coverage is expected to be to our west 
closer to I-95, with more isolated to scattered coverage across 
the Coastal Plain but will continue to monitor trends in the CAM
guidance and adjust PoPs accordingly. 

Tonight into Monday the trough will remain stalled to our west 
and gradually weaken. This reduces the potential for height 
falls over the region despite the trough creeping a bit closer. 
Still, we should see embedded shortwaves moving through aloft. 
Slightly better forcing, paired with another night/day of long 
skinny CAPEs and PWATs north of 2" brings higher precip chances 
compared to this afternoon with heavy rainfall rates, a low end
wet microburst threat, and slow storm motion vectors. All this 
brings flash flooding concerns to mind, especially with how much
rain has been observed in many locations in the past 1-2 weeks.
A Flood Watch has been issued for coastal NC, starting at 11 PM
Sunday and ending 5 PM Monday. There has been some consistency
in guidance showing a shortwave moving through coastal NC
overnight into Monday, bringing numerous to widespread heavy
showers and thunderstorms. HREF and REFS probs of >1" of rain
are over 50% the flood watch region, increasing to 60-80% for
Hatteras Island, Ocracoke, Carteret county, and coastal Onslow
county. Reasonable worst case scenarios show 2-5" of rain in 
the Flood Watch region, although higher values are possible
where heavy rain rates linger with slow storm motions. 

We have been upgraded to a Slight (level 2/5) Excessive Rain 
Outlook for Sunday and Monday with best chances at seeing flash 
flooding likely along Hwy 17 and points east.

Beyond Monday, the trough/low is still expected to linger to our 
west until eventually it gets picked up and shifted to our north by 
another trough moving through the Great Lakes region. As a result, 
daily elevated precip chances continue through mid-week with a low 
end risk for flash flooding. By the end of the week it looks like we 
return back to climo or below climo PoPs as a lack of mid level 
shortwaves or significant forcing will be noted across ENC though we 
do begin to warm back up with temps returning to the upper 80s to 
low 90s inland and mid 80s along the OBX.
